description: The Ambreshwar Shiva Temple, also called Shiv Mandir or Puratana Shivalaya, stands on the bank of the Waldhuni river in Ambarnath, Thane district, about 2 km from Ambarnath railway station (east). According to Wikipedia, it is a basalt temple in the bhumija style, dated to 1060 AD and probably built by the Shilahara king Chhittaraja, possibly rebuilt by his son Mummuni. Its distinctive feature is a sanctum set below the level of the hall, reached by roughly twenty steps and open to the sky. The tower stops just above the hall roof and appears never to have been finished. The three-porched hall retains damaged carvings of divine and female figures. Shiva is the deity, and Maha Shivratri is the festival listed by Wikipedia.

sources.what_it_supports: Location, Waldhuni river bank, ~2 km from station, Shiva, 1060 AD, Shilahara Chhittaraja/Mummuni (probable), bhumija basalt style, sunken open-to-sky sanctum, unfinished shikhara, carvings, Maha Shivratri. No management or official site named.

notes: Description rests on a single source (Wikipedia) because it was the only page opened that gave detail; other search hits (freepressjournal, newsbharati, nativeplanet, sanskritimagazine) appeared only in search results and were not opened. Wikipedia's builder attribution is hedged ('probably'); kept hedged. Wikipedia lists no official website and no managing trust, so official_website null and no timings. Wikipedia's name-meaning ('sky') speculation is uncited, omitted. Portal city/state (Ambarnath, Maharashtra) looks correct; spelling also appears as Ambernath. Reviewer should find a second source (ASI/Maharashtra Archaeology or district page) and any managing trust.

description: The Belbaug temple complex is a Vishnu temple in Pune's old peth area, listed in the Pune Municipal Corporation Grade I heritage list as the Belbaug Temple Complex and Garden, at Belbaug Chowk off Laxmi Road in Budhwar Peth. The same list describes it as an 18th century Vishnu temple, and Wikipedia's list of Hindu temples in Pune says it was built by Nana Fadnavis in the late 1700s. The portal calls it a Lakshmi-Narayan temple; the sources opened here name only Vishnu, so the exact form of the deity and the temple's architecture were not confirmed. No managing trust or official website could be established from the sources reviewed.

description: Dulya Maruti is a Hanuman (Maruti) temple in Pune's old city, at the junction of Laxmi Road and Jagtap Road in Ganesh Peth. Wikipedia's list of Hindu temples in Pune describes it as one of the historic Maruti temples and as one of the city's guardian deities. A devotional aggregator describes a stone temple with a black-stone Hanuman image about five feet tall, along with a Navagraha shrine, a Ram Darbar and a Shivling with Nandi, and ties the shrine to Samarth Ramdas. Its age is given inconsistently there, so no date is stated here. No official website or trust page could be confirmed, and the aggregator's visiting hours were not adopted.

sources.what_it_supports: Dulya Maruti listed as a historic Maruti temple and one of the city's guardian deities.

Aggregator, used only for location (Laxmi Road/Jagtap Road, Ganesh Peth) and physical description (black-stone Hanuman, Navagraha, Ram Darbar, Shivling); also Ramdas attribution, flagged as tradition.

description: ISKCON Juhu, also known as Hare Krishna Land, is a Krishna temple complex near Juhu beach in Mumbai. Its principal deities are Sri Sri Radha Rasabihari, Sri Sri Gaura-Nitai and Sri Sri Sita Rama Laxman Hanuman, which the temple says A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada installed himself. The site says Prabhupada acquired the land in the early 1970s, when the area was remote, and that the Radha Rasabihari deities were first kept in a modest shed before the complex opened in 1978. The four-acre grounds have a marble temple, an auditorium, a restaurant and a guest house. The temple's website also hosts daily darshan and live-stream pages, and offers donation and seva options.

description: Kasba Ganpati is a Ganesh temple in Kasba Peth, the old core of Pune, regarded as the city's gramdevata, or village deity. According to Wikipedia and a Free Press Journal feature, tradition holds that a self-manifested Ganesh image was found in Pune in the 1630s and that Jijabai had the temple built; the Peshwas are said to have added wooden work in the Wada style. The deity is honoured as Pune's first Manacha (most revered) Ganpati, and its mandal leads the final-day immersion procession of the public Ganesh festival. Wikipedia names Shri Kasba Ganpati Mandal as the celebrating group; the Free Press Journal says a Kasba Ganpati Mandal Trust runs the temple and festival.

description: The Mumbadevi Temple stands in the Bhuleshwar and Zaveri Bazaar area of South Mumbai, set among busy markets. It is dedicated to the goddess Mumba, a local form of Parvati and a guardian of the Koli fishing community; a popular etymology links the name of Mumbai to her. The temple trust says the present shrine dates from the 18th century and was first built at Bori Bunder before being rebuilt at Zaveri Bazaar, while Wikipedia gives conflicting dates. Wikipedia describes a black stone image of the goddess with a silver crown, with Annapurna and a tiger vahana nearby. The trust site also lists shrines of Jagadamba, Annapurna and Hanuman, and says it is managed by Shree Mumbadevi Mandir Charities, a registered public charitable trust.

description: Pataleshwar is a rock-cut Shiva temple on Jangali Maharaj Road in Shivajinagar, Pune, carved out of a single mass of basalt. Wikipedia assigns it to the Rashtrakuta period, around the 8th century CE, and notes that it was recorded in 19th-century surveys under names such as Bhamburda and Panchaleshvara. A short approach leads to a sunken courtyard where a circular Nandi pavilion with sixteen pillars stands before the main cave. The hall has a pillared porch and three sanctums, now with Shiva, Parvati and Ganesha, and a passage circles them. Parts look unfinished. Wikipedia says it is a protected monument looked after by the Archaeological Survey of India, and a heritage page says entry is free.

description: The Shitaladevi Temple is in Mahim, in western Mumbai, at the junction of Lady Jamshedji Road and Sitaladevi Temple Road. It honours Sitala, the goddess linked in Hindu tradition with fevers, rashes and smallpox, and often shown as a cooling, healing figure carrying a broom, winnow and pot of water. A Vithoba and Rakhumai shrine stands in front, with the goddess behind it, and the compound also has a shrine to Shantadurga. The temple's origins are unclear. One writer speculates that Raja Bimbadev brought the goddess to Mahim from Kelwe in the 13th century, but admits there is no firm evidence. A Mumbai Metro Line 3 station nearby is named after the temple.

description: The Chaturshringi Temple stands on a hill slope along Senapati Bapat Road in Pune. Its presiding goddess is Chaturshringi, also called Ambareshwari, and Wikipedia says she is regarded as the city's presiding deity, with Durga and Ganesha shrines and miniature Ashtavinayaka figures in the complex. According to Wikipedia, a legend credits a merchant devotee of the goddess Saptashrungi of Vani with finding a self-formed image of the goddess here after she appeared in a dream. The temple is said to date to the time of Shivaji. Reaching the goddess means climbing over two hundred steps, and a government tourism page notes fountains, a waterfall and pilgrim lodgings on the premises. A fair is held at the foot of the hill around Navratri.

description: The Jivdani Mata Temple crowns a hill in eastern Virar, on the northern edge of the Mumbai region in Palghar district. The goddess Jivdani is described by Wikipedia as an avatar of Mahadevi. According to the legend it records, the Pandavas worshipped here during their exile and a herdsman later found the goddess by following a cow up the hill; the original sanctum is a hollow in a cave niche, while the present marble image is a recent installation. Devotees climb a long flight of steps, about 1,465 per Wikipedia and 1,375 per the Palghar district site, and a hilltop fort and a Krishna shrine are nearby. Crowds gather on Sundays and during Navratri, and a fair is held at Dussehra.

description: The Prabhadevi temple stands in the Prabhadevi neighbourhood of Mumbai, between Dadar and Worli, and the locality takes its name from the goddess. The deity is Prabhavati Devi, earlier known as Shakambari Devi. According to Wikipedia, the main idol dates to the 12th century while the present temple was raised in 1715. Folklore holds that the goddess appeared in a dream to Shyam Nayak, a Pathare Prabhu devotee, who then built the shrine. The Pathare Prabhu community site adds that the idols were hidden during Mughal invasions and that a trust formed by Nayak's descendants, the Kirtikar family, manages the temple. An annual ten-day festival is held in the month of Paush, beginning on Shakhambari Purnima.

description: Sarasbaug Ganpati, formally the Shree Siddhivinayak temple, lies in Pune near the foot of Parvati hill. Wikipedia explains that after the Devdeveshwar temple on Parvati was completed in the 18th century, Balaji Baji Rao had a lake built at its base with a small island in the middle, later turned into a garden that Nanasaheb Peshwa named Sarasbaug. According to the same source, Sawai Madhavrao Peshwa built a small temple on the island in 1784 and installed an idol of Siddhivinayak Gajanan, a form of Ganesha. The shrine therefore sits within a garden set in a lake, and it draws large crowds on Ganesh Chaturthi. Wikipedia does not say who manages the temple.

sources.what_it_supports: Location near Parvati hill, lake and island garden, naming by Nanasaheb Peshwa, 1784 temple by Sawai Madhavrao Peshwa, idol of Siddhivinayak Gajanan, festival crowds. No management or website.

description: Shree Vajreshwari Yogini Devi temple is in the village of Vajreshwari (also called Vajrabai), in Bhiwandi taluka of Thane district, near the Tansa river and roughly 75 km from Mumbai. It is dedicated to the goddess Vajreshwari. Wikipedia credits its construction to Chimaji Appa and gives 1739 as the completion year. Outlook Traveller recounts the local tradition that Chimaji Appa, before attacking the Portuguese-held Vasai Fort, prayed to the goddess and vowed to build a grand temple if he won. The shrine is reached by a steep climb. The area is also known for its hot springs, including the Akloli Kund about a kilometre away, reputed locally to have curative properties.

sources.what_it_supports: Thane district location, about 75 km from Mumbai; built by Chimaji Appa, completed 1739 (article tagged unsourced). No management or website.

description: Siddhivinayak at Siddhatek is the second shrine of the Ashtavinayak circuit, set on a hillock on the northern bank of the Bhima river in Karjat taluka of Ahmednagar district (now also called Ahilyanagar). The deity is a self-manifested Ganesha image whose trunk turns to the right, which Wikipedia describes as unique among the eight shrines; the temple site describes it as roughly three feet tall, facing north, with Riddhi and Siddhi on one lap. According to tradition recounted on the trust's site, Vishnu worshipped Ganesha here before defeating the demons Madhu and Kaitabha and attained siddhi, giving the place its name. Wikipedia credits the present temple to Ahilyabai Holkar and says the Chinchwad Devasthan Trust manages it. Devotees often walk circuits around the hill.

description: Walkeshwar Temple and the Banganga Tank lie together on Malabar Hill in South Mumbai, a few dozen metres from the sea. The temple is dedicated to Shiva. Wikipedia says it was built in 1127 by Lakshman Prabhu, a minister of the Silhara kings, damaged by the Portuguese in the 16th century and rebuilt in 1715 by the Gaud Saraswat merchant Rama Kamat, who also funded work on the tank. According to legend, Rama made a sand lingam here on his way to Lanka and shot an arrow into the ground to bring forth the water; the tank's name means Ganga from an arrow. The Gaud Saraswat Temple Trust owns the complex, and the tank is the setting for lamp-lighting at Dev Diwali.

description: Tulshibaug Ram Mandir stands in the Tulshibaug market precinct of Pune's old city, Maharashtra, and is dedicated to Lord Ram. According to Wikipedia, the sanctum holds images of Ram, Sita and Lakshmana, with Hanuman and Ganapati-Parvati also installed, and the precinct includes smaller shrines to Ganesh, Vitthal-Rukmini, Dattatreya and Shiva. Wikipedia says it was commissioned in the Peshwa era by Naro Appaji Khire, a Pune subedar, and that it is managed by Shree Ramji Sansthan. Atlas Obscura notes that the site takes its name from a tulsi garden that once stood here, and describes a tall spire, a nagarkhana (drum house) over the northern gateway and wall murals. Wikipedia mentions a restoration project begun in 2009.

description: Swaminarayan Akshardham is a large mandir complex in Sector 20 of Gandhinagar, Gujarat, built by the Bochasanwasi Shri Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS). Its official site describes it as a tribute to Bhagwan Swaminarayan and to the avatars, devas and sages of Hinduism, and says the carved sandstone mandir holds over 200 murtis. According to the same site it opened on 30 October 1992, was inspired by Yogiji Maharaj and was created under Pramukh Swami Maharaj. Besides the mandir, the campus has exhibitions, an Abhishek Mandapam where visitors may offer abhishek, Nilkanth Vatika, themed gardens and an evening Sat-Chit-Anand water show. The visitor page lists the complex as closed on Mondays.
timings_official: Tuesday to Sunday, closed Monday. Mandir darshan 10:00 am to 7:30 pm (arti 10:00 am and 6:30 pm); exhibitions ticket window 10:30 am to 5:30 pm; Abhishek Mandapam 10:30 am to 7:00 pm; water show after sunset (listed 7:30 pm). Source: akshardham.com/gujarat/visitor-info.

description: The Swaminarayan Mandir at Vadtal, in Kheda district, Gujarat, is described by its own site as the headquarters of the Laxmi Narayan Dev Gadi, one of the two seats of the Swaminarayan tradition (the other being at Ahmedabad). According to Wikipedia, Swaminarayan had it built at the request of local devotees, with Brahmanand Swami supervising, and installed the images himself on 3 November 1824, a date the temple site also gives. The central shrine is for Laxminarayan Dev, with Radha Krishna, Harikrishna Maharaj and other deities in side shrines. The building is lotus-shaped with nine domes and carved pillars. The complex includes a dharamshala and Gnyanbaug garden, and the site offers live darshan and daily darshan updates.

description: Shree Swaminarayan Mandir Kalupur stands in the old city of Ahmedabad, Gujarat, and is presented by its own site as the first shrine of the Swaminarayan Sampraday. According to Wikipedia, Swaminarayan assigned Anandanand Swami to oversee its construction, the land was granted by the British collector John Andrew Dunlop, and it was inaugurated on 24 February 1822. Nar Narayan is enshrined at the centre, with Radha Krishna and other deities beside. The building is noted for Burma teak carving, a sabha mandap on sixty pillars and a mansion added in 1871. Wikipedia and the temple site both describe it as the seat of the Nar Narayan Dev Gadi, one of the two Gadis of the Sampraday; the Vadtal temple belongs to the other.

description: Shri Swaminarayan Mandir at Gadhada (also called Gadhpur), in Gujarat, is known as Gopinathji Dev Mandir and is dedicated to Radha Krishna. According to Wikipedia, Swaminarayan founded it as one of six temples he built, on land donated through the court of Dada Khachar, and the images were installed on 9 October 1828. The central shrine holds Gopinath, Radha and Harikrishna, with a western shrine for Swaminarayan's parents and Vasudeva and an eastern shrine for Revati-Baldevji, Krishna and Suryanarayan. Wikipedia describes a two-storey building with three domes on a high plinth, with halls, dharamshalas and kitchens, and reports that the spires were gold-plated in 2012. Its listing on the Kalupur temple's site presents it as one of that Gadi's mandirs.

description: At Sarangpur (also spelled Salangpur) in Gujarat's Botad area stands a Hanuman shrine where the deity is worshipped as Kashtabhanjan Dev, the remover of sorrows. According to Wikipedia and Gujarat Tourism, the image was installed by Gopalanand Swami, and it belongs to the Vadtal Gadi of the Swaminarayan Sampradaya, unusually for a Swaminarayan site with Hanuman as the main deity. Tradition holds that the image drives away evil spirits, and Saturdays draw many visitors seeking relief for afflicted relatives. Wikipedia describes the idol as a stout figure with a moustache, Shani beneath its foot. A smaller shrine to Swaminarayan stands beside it. A large Hanuman statue was unveiled on the grounds in 2023, as reported by Wikipedia.

description: Girnar is a hill near Junagadh in Gujarat that has a cluster of Jain temples on a ledge along its western face, reached by a climb of roughly 3,500 to 4,000 steps according to Wikipedia. The hill is sacred to both Svetambara and Digambara Jains. The central shrine is dedicated to Neminath, the 22nd Tirthankara, and houses a large black image. Wikipedia describes it as a west-facing granite temple in the Maru-Gurjara style, with a court of 67 shrine cells, rebuilt in 1129 CE and later gilded in 1364 CE. Wikipedia also notes that scholar Madhusudan Dhaky rejects several popular attributions of the other temples there. The Anandji Kalyanji Trust is named as the governing body.

description: Taranga is a hill complex near Kheralu in Mehsana district, Gujarat, with Jain temples and older Buddhist remains. The main shrine is dedicated to Ajitnath, the second Tirthankara, and holds a large white marble image. Wikipedia says the temple, built in the Maru-Gurjara style of sandstone and brick, was completed in 1161 under the Solanki king Kumarapala at the urging of Hemachandra, though its own infobox gives a different year. The compounds hold 14 Svetambara and 5 Digambara temples. Gujarat Tourism notes that the hill also has Buddhist-era shrines to Taranamata, and that visiting involves a trek. Wikipedia names the Anandji Kalyanji Trust as the governing body of the Svetambara temple.

description: Junagarh Fort stands in Bikaner, Rajasthan, and is a palace-fort complex rather than a single temple. According to Incredible India, Rao Bika laid its foundation in 1478 and Raja Rai Singh expanded it, with work finishing in 1594. A Government of India fort listing describes Har Mandir inside the fort as the chapel where the royal family worshipped its deities. The fort also holds palaces such as Karan Mahal, Phool Mahal and Anup Mahal, and a museum in Ganga Mahal. Its gateways include Karan Pol and Suraj Pol. The Incredible India page mentions Laxmi Nath, Karni Mata and Kalika Mata temples as sights elsewhere in Bikaner city, not inside the fort. No separate temple trust is named in the sources.

description: Luna Vasahi is a Jain temple in the Dilwara group near Mount Abu in Sirohi district, Rajasthan, dedicated to Neminatha, the 22nd Tirthankara. According to Wikipedia, the brothers Vastupal and Tejpal, ministers of the Vaghela ruler Virdhaval, built it in 1230 in memory of their brother Lunig, modelling it on the earlier Vimal Vasahi. Its marble work includes a domed hall with a hanging pendant, a band of 72 seated Tirthankaras, a hathishala with ten elephants and about 47 sub-shrines. A black marble image of Neminatha stands in the sanctum. Wikipedia names the Seth Kalyanji Parmanandji Pedhi as the managing trust, with inconsistent spelling in the article.

description: Vimal Vasahi is one of the five Jain temples of the Dilwara (Delwara) complex, set in the village of Dilwara about 2.5 km from Mount Abu in Sirohi district, Rajasthan. Its principal image is Rishabhanatha (Adinatha), the first tirthankara. According to Wikipedia, it was commissioned by Vimal Shah, a minister of the Chaulukya king Bhima I, in the early eleventh century. The shrine is built wholly of white marble and stands in an open courtyard ringed by a corridor of small cells holding tirthankara images. Its pillars, arches and lotus-patterned ceilings are carved in fine detail, with scenes from Jain mythology. Wikipedia says the complex is managed by the Seth Shri Kalyanji Parmanandji Pedhi.

description: Haldeshwar Mahadev is a Shiva shrine in the Chhappan hills of the Aravalli range, at the foot of Piploon village near Siwana in Balotra district, Rajasthan. According to the legend recorded on Wikipedia, a demon named Haldia troubled the hills until Shiva appeared beneath a peepal tree and killed him, giving the place its name. The same source mentions a cave and sacred fire (dhuni) associated with the saint Gorakhnath on a hill at the site, a tradition that the Pandavas spent part of their exile here, and a Bhawani temple on a higher nearby hill. Reaching the temple is described as a trek across seven hills, and crowds gather especially in the month of Saavan.

description: Muchhal Mahavir is a Shvetambara Jain temple at Ghanerao in Pali district, Rajasthan, on the route from Falna towards Kumbhalgarh. It is dedicated to Mahavir and is listed with Ranakpur, Narlai, Nadol and Varkana in the Gorwad group of five pilgrimage sites. The name means Mahavir with a moustache. According to Jain tradition recorded on Wikipedia, a Mewar ruler saw a hair on the image, and the deity is said to have shown a moustache after the priest fasted. The temple is in Nagara style, with a carved entrance arch and two black stone elephants outside the door. A dharamshala and dining hall serve pilgrims, and Wikipedia says the Anandji Kalyanji Trust governs it.

description: Pandupol Hanuman Temple is a Hanuman shrine in Alwar district, Rajasthan, in the Aravalli hills in the Sariska area. Its sanctum holds a reclining image of Hanuman. The name comes from a Mahabharata legend, retold on the Incredible India site, in which Bhima, during the Pandavas' exile, met an old monkey blocking his path who turned out to be Hanuman. Bhima is said to have made an opening in the rocks through which the Pandavas passed, hence Pandupol. Devotees come in large numbers on Tuesdays and Saturdays, and a fair known as the Lakhi Mela is held during Chaitra Navratri. The tourism page does not say who manages the temple.

description: Narlai is a village in Desuri tehsil, Pali district, Rajasthan, which Wikipedia identifies with the Nadulagarika named in twelfth-century Chahamana inscriptions and describes as a trading centre. A listing site for Jain temples says the village has about twelve ancient Jain temples. One of them, the Neminath Shwetambar Mandir, stands at the foot of the Shatrunjay Tirth hill. Although named for Neminath, its main image is described there as Sogathiya Parshwanath, said to have emerged from the ground, and the temple is usually kept locked, with keys held at the office of the main Adinath temple. Narlai is also counted among the five pilgrimage sites of the Gorwad region, alongside Ranakpur, Ghanerao, Nadol and Varkana.
